name: Bundism
summary: Bundism is the doctrine of the General Jewish Labour Bund (1897-1948): a secular Marxist socialism of the Jewish working class that demanded democracy and class struggle together with national-cultural autonomy, equal language rights and Yiddish schools for Jews where they live (doikayt, 'hereness'). It rejected Zionism, emigration and Hebrew revival, rejected assimilation as an aim, and opposed Bolshevik single-party rule while building unions, schools and armed self-defence against pogroms.
scope: The Jewish Labour Bund in the Russian Empire and interwar Poland, from its 1897 founding to the Second World War, using its own programmatic texts (Our Demands, the 1899, 1905 and 1910 resolutions), Vladimir Medem's writings on the national question and social democracy, and the scholarship on them. Later diaspora Bundist groups, the Russian Social Democratic movement and the wider Jewish or socialist camps are used only to date events and are not a source of positions.

public-ownership.rationale: Medem's explanation of the social-democratic programme names the final aim as moving factories, mines and land from private to common ownership, with all working for the common good under society's direction.

property-fundamental.rationale: The programme's final aim is to end private ownership of factories, mines and land, so private property in the means of production is something to override, not a right that is hard to override.

unions-good.rationale: The Bund grew out of Jewish strike funds and trade unions and built and led the Jewish union movement in Russia and Poland (about 99,000 members in 1939), treating union organisation as the core of its work.

class-collaboration.rationale: The Bund's demands hold that on economic and political questions the struggle follows class interests, bourgeois against proletarian, and Medem calls class struggle the only principle of social democracy.

workers-own-party.rationale: The Bund was founded as the party of the Jewish working class, and Medem presents the social-democratic party as the open party of one class, the workers.

revolution-justified.rationale: The Bund was founded to organise Jewish workers for socialist and revolutionary ends and took a leading part in the 1905 revolution against the tsarist autocracy.

political-violence-never.rationale: The Bund took part in revolution against the tsar and organised armed self-defence against pogroms, and one of its members shot the governor of Vilna in 1902.

democracy-best.rationale: Medem's programme demands full popular rule in a democratic republic, and the Bund split from the Bolsheviks over democracy in party and government, calling the 1917 seizure of power authoritarian.

one-party-rule.rationale: The Bund opposed Lenin's rule from 1901 over democracy in a socialist party and government, called the 1917 seizure of power authoritarian, and was itself suppressed by the single-party state.

suppress-opposition.rationale: The programme Medem describes demands the broadest political freedoms, and the Bund opposed the Bolshevik regime that suppressed independent parties, itself included.

party-controls-media.rationale: Medem lists freedom of assembly, press and speech among the political freedoms social democracy demands, and the Bund fought the Bolshevik single-party state that took control of the press.

elective-rulers.rationale: The programme demands a democratic republic with full rule by the people in place of the tsarist autocracy.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: The programme demands a democratic republic, and the Bund fought the autocracy as the central obstacle for Jewish and all workers.

sacred-ruler.rationale: The Bund fought the tsarist autocracy, and its programme puts all political power in the people in a democratic republic.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Medem's programme places authority in the people, 'complete rule of the people', and the Bund was a secular party that fought religious Orthodoxy.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The programme Medem describes demands the abolition of all civil, political and national inequality, which includes the old estate privileges.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Medem's programme requires full rule by the people through a democratic republic and universal political freedoms.

state-harmful.rationale: The Bund wanted a democratic state that guarantees rights, labour protection and equal national language and school rights, not the absence of the state.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The programme calls for state labour protection (eight-hour day, weekly rest, insurance) and the Bund demanded state schools in each nation's language, which go beyond defence, justice and property.

total-state.rationale: The Bund's demands take education and culture out of the hands of the state and give them to each nationality, so that the state has nothing to do with cultural interests.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The programme demands the abolition of all civil, political and national inequality, and the Bund put equal civil rights for Jews on its banner.

racial-franchise.rationale: The Bund demanded equal political rights regardless of nationality, and Medem's state of nationalities gives citizenship equally to all nationalities.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: The programme calls for abolishing all national inequality, and the Bund fought the discriminatory laws that kept Jews apart in the Pale.

property-franchise.rationale: The programme demands full popular rule in a democratic republic and the abolition of all political inequality, which excludes a property bar on voting.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: The Polish Bund voted for the dictatorship of the proletariat and the Comintern in 1920, then joined the Socialist International in 1930, and its factions split over it for years.

workers-councils.rationale: The Polish Bund backed government of the Soviets in 1920, but it later sat in parliaments and municipal councils and its left and right factions stayed divided over the question.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: National-cultural autonomy, with schools and culture run by each nation itself and the state kept out, was the Bund's programme from 1901 and Medem's central proposal.

minority-language-support.rationale: The Bund's 1910 conference demanded that all state institutions use the local languages, state schools for each group in its own language, and equal status for Yiddish.

single-official-language.rationale: The Bund rejected any ranking of languages into dominant and tolerated ones and demanded Yiddish a status equal to Russian in assemblies and public life.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Medem's state of nationalities, which the Bund adopted, separates citizenship from nationality so that several nations live equally in one state, against the nation-state ideal.

national-self-determination.rationale: Medem rejected the nation-state as the answer for mixed regions, called the demand for separate national states a bourgeois solution, and held that separation only helps the national majority.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Medem's neutralism took no side on whether Jewish culture should survive, and the Bund later (from about 1910 and in interwar Poland) actively built Yiddish culture, so the evidence points both ways.

sacred-nation.rationale: Medem called reverence for one's own nationality, 'ours is a temple', the common essence of all nationalisms, and Erlich rejected the idea of Jews as a chosen people.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Medem holds that national cultures share the same human content in different forms, that no nationality should be privileged, and Erlich rejected the claim that Jews were a chosen people.

workers-nation.rationale: The Bund organised Jewish workers separately in a national party yet put international class solidarity above national solidarity and refused alliances with nationalist parties, and scholars describe this as a standing tension.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: The Bund's 1905 congress called an independent Jewish territory utopian and adventurist and resolved to fight Zionism in all its forms, though after 1947 the Bund accepted Israel's existence while denying it any special importance.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: The Bund's doctrine of doikayt held that Jews should fight for equal rights and socialism where they live, opposed emigration as a solution and rejected the Zionist territory.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: The Bund campaigned against the anti-Jewish economic boycott in Poland.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: The Bund campaigned against the ousting of Jewish workers from their jobs and against the anti-Jewish boycott in Poland.

more-religion-public.rationale: The Bund was a secular party that conducted a relentless campaign against religious Orthodoxy and demanded secularisation of Jewish communal life.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: The Bund demanded secularisation and democratisation of Jewish communal life and campaigned against religious Orthodoxy, which rules out law founded on scripture.

clerical-rule.rationale: The Bund fought Orthodox religious leadership and demanded secularised, democratic community institutions.

missingStatements.text: Workers belonging to a religious minority should have a legal right to rest on their own weekly day of rest.
missingStatements.rationale: The Bund demanded the Sabbath rest day for Jewish workers as a general Jewish right and pressed for freedom of rest on the Sabbath in 1910.

missingStatements.text: A persecuted minority should organise its own self-defence against mob violence rather than wait for the authorities to protect it.
missingStatements.rationale: The Bund became a main organiser of Jewish self-defence against pogroms in 1903-06 and again in the 1930s, and its self-defence squads broke up several planned pogroms.

notes: Scope is the Bund up to 1939; the post-1947 Bund (accepting Israel while rejecting its special status, a 'neutralist' line on the Arab-Israeli conflict) is used only to qualify the Israel answer. Searched: national question, language, schools, religion and secularism, Zionism and emigration, democracy and Bolshevism, unions and self-defence, the Comintern split, interwar Poland. Medem's 1918 pamphlet on parties explains the social-democratic programme in general; its programme answers carry medium confidence because the Bund's own programme texts found are limited to the national question. Medem's 1904 text itself was read through Gechtman because the English and Yiddish text were not available as full text. Most themes (family, gender, sexuality, ecology, technology, tax, welfare, foreign policy) are null because the sources record no Bundist position.
